item.title: Researchers Discover Hidden Backdoor in 20 Router Models Allowing Remote Root Access
item.description:
A vendor-built backdoor named ENDLESSDOORS ships across 20 Zbtlink router models, granting unauthenticated remote root access via outbound connections that bypass firewalls entirely. No patch exists.
- ENDLESSDOORS is built on rctl, a dormant 2015 open-source tool. Two userland processes masquerade as kernel threads named kworker (unbracketed, with real memory footprints) and launch automatically at boot via an init script called skworker. The implant dials out, so NAT and perimeter firewalls offer zero protection.
- The protocol is deliberately minimal: the router sends a 39-byte hello containing a class label and its LAN MAC address, with no handshake, no key exchange, and no verification. The server responds with shell commands executed as uid 0 via popen(). The reserved string rctlbash opens a second connection to port 7001 and spawns a live /bin/sh pseudo-terminal root shell.
- Four C2 endpoints serve the entire affected fleet: zbtctl.epplink[.]net resolving to 47.100.190[.]96 (Alibaba Cloud), hardcoded IP 47.107.224[.]89 (Alibaba Cloud), online-string[.]com resolving to 45.32.81[.]152 (Vultr), and rbdg4nzqadui.wikaba[.]com resolving to 43.248.136[.]125 (Jiangsu Dongyun Cloud).
- Zbtlink markets hardware under Wiflyer, ZBT, and ZBTWiFi on Amazon, Alibaba, and Shopify. The vendor claims the backdoor was a maintenance feature limited to sample units, then quietly pulled firmware downloads, undermining that explanation.

item.title: When Agentic Glue Melts: Exploiting Cloudflare Code Mode and Workers
item.description:
Five memory-corruption bugs in workerd, the runtime behind Cloudflare Workers and Code Mode, enable cross-tenant secret theft and sandbox escape to host RCE. Two rated Critical by Cloudflare. Patched in production; self-hosted deployments must update to v1.20260619.1.
Key findings:
- The attack surface is workerd's JSG layer, the C++ glue marshaling JavaScript calls into native code. Unlike V8, JSG had almost no prior public scrutiny, and the objects it allocates land on the tcmalloc heap, outside both the V8 sandbox cage and memory-protection keys. That means a bug there is not boxed in the way a V8 bug would be. Check Point found five bugs: two UAFs (node:zlib deflateParams and HTMLRewriter AttributesIterator), two URLPattern out-of-bounds reads, and a KV SQL authorizer bypass leading to arbitrary deserialization of attacker-controlled bytes into workerd's internal structured-clone deserializer.
- Cross-tenant secret theft via URLPattern OOB: a nested capture group like /(ab(cde))/ causes V8 to report two capture groups while nameList holds only one name. The loop reads 24 bytes past the vector end, treats them as a kj::String, and dereferences ptr, returning bytes at an attacker-chosen address. Using tcmalloc free-list layout and VFS file buffers as stable in-place primitives, one Worker can sweep the shared heap and read another tenant's secrets (Bearer tokens, private keys) without touching the cage or MPK-protected pages.

item.title: OctLurk and SilkLurk: Analysis of a Modular Cyber Espionage Framework
item.description:
Chinese-linked espionage campaign deploys two undocumented backdoors, OctLurk and SilkLurk, against government and public-sector targets across Central Asia and the Middle East, with Afghanistan and Syria also in scope.
Key findings:
- OctLurk and SilkLurk are modular backdoors sharing a plugin-based architecture that allows operators to extend capability post-compromise. Both use victim-specific decryption keys and heavy obfuscation, meaning a sample pulled from one victim will not decrypt cleanly on another, complicating bulk sandbox analysis.
- In-memory execution is central to both families, reducing on-disk footprint and making traditional file-hash hunting unreliable. Responders should prioritize memory forensics and look for anomalous injected modules in trusted processes.
- LurkProxy is a companion traffic-proxying utility used to route attacker C2 communications, obscuring true infrastructure. Network defenders should flag internal hosts making repeated, low-volume outbound connections to uncommon ports, consistent with proxy relay behavior.
- Targeted verticals include Ministries of Foreign Affairs, Law Enforcement, Healthcare, Research, and Logistics, indicating intelligence-collection intent rather than disruption. PlugX is listed as a related family, suggesting shared tooling or operator overlap with known Chinese 🇨🇳 espionage clusters.
Prioritize memory acquisition on compromised hosts before remediation.

item.title: ChainDrop: Inside a Self-Propagating npm Worm
item.description:
ChainDrop is a self-propagating npm worm that steals GitHub Actions runner secrets and uses Ethereum smart contracts for C2, marking a shift in supply chain attack sophistication.
- ChainDrop spreads by compromising npm packages and injecting malicious code that executes during install-time lifecycle hooks (postinstall), targeting any developer or CI/CD pipeline that installs an infected dependency.
- The worm targets GitHub Actions runner environments specifically, extracting secrets and tokens from the runner context, meaning a single poisoned dependency in a workflow can expose repository secrets, cloud credentials, and signing keys.
- C2 routing uses Ethereum smart contracts rather than hardcoded domains or IPs, making traditional domain-based blocklists and DNS sinkholes ineffective. The attacker updates the C2 endpoint by writing to the blockchain, and the malware reads it on-chain.
- For DFIR, key artifacts include postinstall scripts in package.json, unexpected outbound connections to Ethereum RPC endpoints from CI runners, and anomalous environment variable access (process.env) in Node.js child processes during build jobs.
Audit your npm dependency tree for unexpected postinstall hooks. In GitHub Actions, review runner logs for outbound calls to Ethereum JSON-RPC endpoints and treat any exposed GITHUB_TOKEN or cloud secret as fully compromised. IOC list and full technical details in the Unit 42 report.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2085501984052789623

item.title: UNC6671 Rebrands: Multi-Brand Vishing Extortion Targets Financial Services and Enterprise Cloud Environments
item.description:
UNC6671 did not retire with BlackFile: it rebranded across Redact, Pink, Helix, and Falcon, accelerating vishing-driven cloud extortion against financial services and private equity targets through mid-2026.
- UNC6671 calls employees on personal mobile numbers, spoofs legitimate helpdesk numbers, and directs victims to AiTM credential-harvesting subdomains (e.g., [company].createssopasskey[.]com, [company].addssopasskey[.]com) to steal M365 and Okta session tokens. Post-compromise, automated scripts exfiltrate SaaS data while operators delete password-reset confirmations, security alerts, and MFA-change notifications to suppress detection (T1070).
- Shared infrastructure ties all five brands together: passkeyhelpdesk[.]com targeted both Falcon and Helix victims simultaneously; setupsso[.]com and idokta[.]com bridged to BlackFile; passkeyms[.]com and mysecurepasskey[.]com bridged to Pink. Domain provisioning accelerated to one every 1.6 days in June-July 2026, with seven domains stood up in a 72-hour window July 20-22.
- Blockchain analysis of 18 BlackFile wallets from January-May 2026 shows 141.65 BTC received (~$10.69M USD). Final payments averaged $750K in over 53% of tracked cases, and payments continued past the May 11 "shutdown" announcement confirming rebranding was financial cover, not retirement.
- Hunt in Okta and Entra ID audit logs for system.multifactor.factor.setup events immediately preceded by user.authentication.auth_via_mfa failures.

item.title: (TLP:CLEAR) Backdoor Identified in Chinese-Made Zbtlink Router Firmware – ENDLESSDOORS
item.description:
Factory-installed C2 backdoor ENDLESSDOORS found in Chinese 🇨🇳 Zbtlink router firmware, giving root shell access to 100,000+ deployed units worldwide with no patch available.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-66747: the ENDLESSDOORS implant is baked into vendor firmware and started at boot by the manufacturer's own init script. It beacons every 35 seconds to hardcoded C2 over unencrypted, unauthenticated channels on ports 7000 and 7001. Anyone controlling the destination, or sitting on the path, gets a root shell. No inbound exposure required: devices behind firewalls are equally compromised.
- Confirmed in 21 firmware images across 20+ models including CPE2801, WE/WG series, and Z8102AX-2DSIM, sold under Zbtlink and Wiflyer brands. No fixed firmware exists and VulnCheck did not pursue coordinated disclosure because the behavior appears intentional.
- For ICS/OT responders, the forensic tell is two userland kworker processes plus the files /usr/sbin/kworker, /usr/lib/librctl.so, /etc/kworker.cfg, and /etc/init.d/skworker on the device.
- Defanged IOCs: zbtctl.epplink[.]net, online-string[.]com, rbdg4nzqadui.wikaba[.]com, 47.100.190[.]96, 47.107.224[.]89, 45.32.81[.]152, 43.248.136[.]125.
Inventory OT edge gear by model number, not brand label. Block the IOCs at egress and DNS, alert on outbound ports 7000/7001 from infrastructure segments, and replace confirmed devices. Suricata, Snort, and YARA rules are in the VulnCheck report.

item.title: (TLP:CLEAR) Vulnerability Notification – N-able N-central Authentication Bypass Actively Exploited
item.description:
CVE-2026-18556 and CVE-2026-18577 (CVSS 8.2) in N-able N-central are actively exploited, giving attackers unauthenticated admin access to RMM servers and every downstream managed endpoint.
- Two auth bypass flaws let an unauthenticated remote attacker gain full administrative control of N-central. N-able confirmed active exploitation on Aug 1, 2026. The first clean build is 2026.3.1.7; upgrading only to 2026.3 is NOT sufficient, as CVE-2026-18577 persisted through 2026.3.1.
- Attackers abused N-central's built-in Take Control feature to reach managed endpoints, then registered a Cloudflare tunnel service for persistent access. Persistence lives on the downstream endpoint, not the RMM server, so patching N-central alone does not evict an attacker already inside.
- Hunt for unexpected cloudflared services or svchost.exe running from a user's Documents folder. Review N-central ui_access_control.log and endpoint logs at C:\ProgramData\GetSupportService_N-Central\Logs\BASupSrvc_*.log.gz for unaccountable Take Control sessions, especially tied to apparent N-able support identities.
- Published IOCs include IPs 173.249.252[.]200, 87.249.138[.]34, 37.19.210[.]32, 37.153.90[.]88, 92.118.112[.]181, 68.235.46[.]214 and domains mousears.synology[.]me and wagoosh.direct.quickconnect[.]to. item.title: ChainDrop Worm Hits 400+ npm Packages with Two Billion Monthly Installs
item.description:
ChainDrop worm poisons 430+ npm packages with 2 billion monthly installs, harvesting cloud and developer credentials through GitHub's own trusted publishing pipeline.
Key findings:
- Attackers compromised a keyv maintainer's GitHub account on August 4, pushed malicious commits directly to the main branch, then cut new releases. GitHub Actions signed them with valid provenance, so the poisoned versions landed on npm looking legitimate. Affected packages include flat-cache (557M downloads/month), file-entry-cache (557M), and cacheable (29M).
- The infostealer targets npm and GitHub tokens, AWS credentials, Kubernetes secrets, HashiCorp Vault tokens, and Stripe and Slack tokens, then performs a broad file system scan. Stolen data is encrypted and exfiltrated to a public GitHub repo described as "Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again."
- Worm propagation is the critical escalation. The malware uses stolen tokens to spread across other maintainers and repositories, chaining compromises through trusted CI/CD workflows. Packages tied to Deliveroo, Picsart, and Qlik were among those hit.
- DFIR scope is wider than direct installs. Even packages installed but not actively used can expose credentials. Treat any installation of an affected version as a credential breach event.
Rotate all developer and cloud credentials on any system that installed affected package versions.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2085245590066348200

item.title: Fake Open VSX Extensions Harvest Private Repo and CI Data
item.description:
77 fake Open VSX extensions squatted real publisher namespaces and beaconed git identity, CI pipeline data, and private repo names to a single attacker-controlled domain, active July 26 to August 1, 2026.
- All 77 packages impersonated real extensions by republishing their names under unauthorized accounts. Squatted namespaces included AMD, Azure, Salesforce OSS, Hyperledger, LEGO Education, a US 🇺🇸 federal agency, and marketplace.visualstudio itself. Every package beaconed to one domain registered just 11 days before the first package appeared, on a three-year term through a registrar that redacts registrant details.
- 19 of the 77 carried a fuller payload: hostname, OS username, machine ID, editor details, git remote host, org name, commit email domain, branch, HEAD commit, GitHub repo name, GitLab project path, and Codespace name. On a build runner that is the full private repository name. The beacon retried for seven days across restarts, and if all HTTP endpoints failed, a DNS TXT query fetched a replacement collector address, letting the operator re-home infrastructure without pushing new packages.
- One extension's telemetry disclosure actively lied: it claimed CI data covered marker names only, never values. The code sent both. The single most sensitive field was the one the disclosure said was withheld.
- Open VSX removed the packages August 3 but the collector infrastructure was still live at time of writing.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2085230532863098881

item.title: 22 Seconds to Compromise: How Automated SSH Actors Move From Login to Persistence Before You Can Blink [Guest Diary], (Thu, Aug 6th)
item.description:
A Cowrie SSH honeypot captured a fully automated intrusion that went from credential auth to persistent backdoor in 22 seconds, part of the ongoing mdrfckr campaign with 93 confirmed active IPs still scanning weeks later.
- At 01:06:43 UTC on May 23, 2026, IP 163.7.8[.]79 (Byteplus, AS150436) authenticated as root using "Aa123123123", then executed a pre-scripted playbook: wiped and recreated .ssh/, injected a backdoor key (SHA256: a8460f446be540410004b1a8db4083773fa46f7fe76fa84219c93daa1669f8f2), changed the root password, and cleared hosts.deny. All of it in 22 seconds. No human hesitation, no exploration.
- The session maps cleanly to T1078 (Valid Accounts), T1098 (Account Manipulation via authorized_keys), T1059 (Command Execution), and T1562 (Impair Defenses). Deleting the existing .ssh dir before re-creating it is the tell: the actor evicts all prior keys to ensure exclusive access.
- 21 successful logins from 21 distinct IPs hit the honeypot in one 24-hour window, clustered 01:00-02:30 UTC, with a coordinated /24 subnet block (80.94.92[.]171, 80.94.92[.]184, 80.94.92[.]186) generating high-volume sessions simultaneously. This is distributed scanning infrastructure, not opportunistic individuals.
- 93 IPs from the documented mdrfckr campaign list were still actively hitting the sensor weeks after first observation. AbuseIPDB shows 163.7.8[.]79 at 100% abuse confidence with 5,700+ reported incidents.

item.title: Don't Revoke That Token Yet: Inside the keyv/cacheable npm Worm, (Wed, Aug 5th)
item.description:
The keyv/cacheable npm worm flips incident response instinct on its head: revoking the stolen npm token does not neutralize the payload, it triggers it.
Key findings:
- The malicious package was designed so that token revocation is the activation condition, not a remediation step. Standard supply-chain IR muscle memory (revoke, rotate, cycle) is weaponized against the responder.
- Any build host that executed the compromised keyv or cacheable package should be treated as fully compromised. Scope your investigation to CI/CD pipeline nodes, not just developer workstations.
- DFIR priority shifts from credential hygiene to artifact preservation: capture memory, process trees, network connections, and filesystem changes before touching any credentials in the environment.
- The worm classification means lateral spread is possible across dependent packages or build environments. Map your dependency graph for keyv and cacheable consumers before containment.
Takeaway: Before revoking anything, image the affected build host and pull network logs. Establish the blast radius first. Token rotation comes after you understand what the payload does on activation, not before. Check the SANS ISC report for the full behavioral breakdown and IOC list.

item.title: The iOS 27 Recovery Menu: What It Means for Forensics
item.description:
iOS 27's new pre-boot recovery menu changes the seizure threat model for mobile examiners, not because it breaks encryption, but because it is three seconds from a factory wipe and auto-joins Wi-Fi before the data volume ever unlocks.
- The menu is reached by powering off, then holding the side button through boot. No cable required, no broken device required. Any healthy iPhone, any user, any time. It contains Erase All Content and Settings, Recovery Assistant (which erased at least one iPhone 11 in beta testing without warning), and Nearby Device Recovery, which can trigger a full restore from a helper phone.
- AFU state is destroyed the moment you enter this menu because it requires a full power cycle. BFU from that point forward. The oldest rule in mobile forensics applies unchanged: do not reboot the evidence.
- The recovery environment auto-joins known Wi-Fi with no credential and no user session. An isolated evidence device that recognizes a lab network can pull a firmware update and move to a version your tooling does not yet support. Faraday from seizure, and audit every network the device has seen.
- Diagnostics Mode will display serial number and IMEI on a locked, unpaired device with no pairing record. Useful for identification when the SIM tray is missing and the case is unreadable. Do not accept the config profile or transmit logs. Data leaving the device is a chain-of-custody event and may alert the account holder.

item.title: TP-Link Omada flaws could allow attackers to infiltrate industrial network infrastructure through zero-touch provisioning
item.description:
15 new flaws in TP-Link Omada's Zero-Touch Provisioning platform chain together to compromise controllers, cloud services, and managed devices across enterprise and industrial networks at scale.
Key findings:
- Hard-coded private keys and TLS certs are the backbone of the chain: CVE-2025-15627 embeds a hardcoded private key in Omada protocol v1, CVE-2025-15628 does the same for a v2 TLS cert, and that same root key signs firmware updates across Omada, Festa, Tapo, Kasa, and VIGI product lines. One key extraction enables MitM across 70+ million app installs.
- The attack chain runs from unauthenticated device adoption to root RCE. An external attacker enumerates sequential serial numbers (FSCT-2025-0011), races the cloud adoption handshake by spoofing a MAC (CVE-2025-15630), harvests credential hashes weakened by empty salts (CVE-2025-9290), then pivots to OS command injection as root via CVE-2025-7850.
- Credential exposure is systemic: site passwords transmit in cleartext (CVE-2025-15544), device passwords are stored as unsalted MD5 encrypted with a hard-coded key (CVE-2025-15631), and the RC4 key protecting v1 protocol traffic is predictable (CVE-2025-15629).
- VIGI surveillance and shared cloud accounts amplify blast radius. A compromised Omada cloud account can pivot into VIGI Cloud VMS, potentially exposing video feeds at critical facilities.

item.title: Weaponizing Windows Updates with NotWSUSpicious
item.description:
SpecterOps releases NotWSUSpicious, a tool that weaponizes enterprise WSUS servers configured with external MSSQL backends, turning the update pipeline into a payload delivery mechanism against any managed endpoint.
Key details:
- The attack requires WSUS to use an external MSSQL server with EPA disabled. PetitPotam coerces the WSUS computer account (WSUS1$) into authenticating to the attacker, ntlmrelayx relays that NTLM auth to MSSQL port 1433 via SOCKS, and a custom mssqlclient.py connects to the SUSDB database as the machine account (T1557.001, T1021.002).
- NotWSUSpicious.py generates the full SQL stored-procedure chain: spImportUpdate, spSaveXmlFragment, spSetBatchURL, spCreateTargetGroup, spAddComputerToTargetGroup, and spDeployUpdate. The tool calculates SHA1 and SHA256 hashes of the payload and injects them into WSUS update metadata so the file passes integrity checks.
- Payload delivery abuses BITS: a bundled BitsWebServer.py serves the malicious file over HTTP range requests, which WSUS fetches natively. The update appears legitimate to the target machine, which executes the payload at next check-in.
- Detection opportunities: anomalous MSSQL sessions authenticating as a computer account (WSUS1$) to the SUSDB database, unexpected rows in SUSDB update tables with attacker-controlled GUIDs, and BITS traffic (HTTP 206 responses) from non-Microsoft hosts serving update files.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2085124682911764782

item.title: Turning Enterprise Update Servers Into Backdoor Factories (0_o) – Part 1
item.description:
WSUS NTLM relay technique weaponizes the upstream server's computer account to inject malicious updates directly into the SUSDB, enabling surgical payload delivery to individual targets without touching a domain controller.

The account lands in the webService database role, which carries EXECUTE on stored procedures but no direct table access, so the entire attack chain runs through stored procedures only.

item.title: Turning Enterprise Update Servers Into Backdoor Factories (0_o) – Part 2
item.description:
WSUS signature verification bypass lets attackers deploy unsigned payloads via enterprise update infrastructure, turning patch management into a persistence mechanism with no user interaction required.
- WSUS enforces digital signature checks on downloaded executables, but Microsoft.UpdateServices.ContentSyncAgent.dll (a .NET assembly in C:\Program Files\Update Services\Services) contains a VerifyFile function that skips CheckCertificateSignature entirely if the filename ends in .txt or .esd. Renaming a payload Ghost.txt is enough to pass verification and trigger a FileVerified log event instead of failure.
- The full attack chain: inject a malicious update via SQL stored procedures (spCreateTargetGroups, spSetBatchURL, spDeployUpdate), host the payload on a BITS-compatible web server supporting Range headers, and deliver it to targeted workgroups. If "Auto download and schedule install" group policy is enabled, zero user interaction is needed.
- WSUS logs at C:\Program Files\Update Services\LogFiles are the primary artifact. Watch for FileVerificationFailed events, then FileVerified events on .txt or .esd filenames. The payload process runs for a few hours then exits, but the update redeploys automatically, creating persistent C2 re-entry.
- The researcher released NotWSUSPicious to automate malicious update creation. Detection: alert on spSetBatchURL calls referencing .txt or .esd files, and spDeployUpdate executions from non-computer accounts.

item.title: Rapid7 Analysis: KindaRails2Shell (CVE-2026-66066)
item.description:
CVE-2026-66066 in Ruby on Rails Active Storage chains an arbitrary file read into RCE via a crafted MAT/HDF5 upload. Actively exploited with a public Metasploit module. Patch immediately.
Key findings:
- Affected versions: Active Storage < 7.2.3.2, >= 8.0 < 8.0.5.1, >= 8.1 < 8.1.3.1. The direct-upload endpoint accepts attacker-controlled content_type and writes it to the blob record without byte inspection. A crafted file stored as image/png passes the variable? gate (database check only, no file bytes examined) and reaches the libvips pipeline. No secret material is needed for the file read stage.

The HDF5 external storage feature then reads attacker-chosen file paths and offsets, returning bytes as image pixels in the rendered PNG response.
- File read escalates to RCE by recovering SECRET_KEY_BASE from /proc/<pid>/environ, then signing a malicious ImageProcessing variation. JSON-safe payloads {"send":["spawn","/bin/sh","-c","cmd"]} reach Kernel via image_processing 1.14.0's Chainable (T1059), confirmed against Rails 8.0.5 with config.active_support.message_serializer = :json.

item.title: Workaround For Duplicate LVM Names
item.description:
Duplicate LVM UUIDs across cloned Linux disk images block simultaneous mounting on a single analysis workstation. xmount's --cache option solves this without touching the original evidence.
Key findings:
- The core problem: Linux images cloned from a master share identical PV UUIDs, VG names, VG UUIDs, and per-filesystem UUIDs. vgscan silently drops the duplicate device, making the second image inaccessible until conflicts are resolved at every layer.
- xmount --cache creates a FUSE-backed virtual disk1.dd and absorbs all destructive metadata changes into a separate cache file. The original raw image MD5 stays unchanged throughout. Verified in the article: md5sum confirmed e3b85cad126731e76955b2240b69f39d before and after all modifications.
- The fix sequence matters: (1) tear down the duplicate loopback before pvchange -u, (2) vgrename plus vgchange -u for the VG, (3) e2fsck -f then tune2fs -U random for each EXT4 logical volume. Skipping any step produces cascading LVM warnings and failed mounts.
- Mount read-only with ro,noexec once UUIDs are resolved. The cache file, not the image, absorbs the 328MB of metadata writes by the time all three filesystems are modified and mounted.
Practitioner takeaway: add xmount --cache to your Linux LVM acquisition workflow now, before you hit this on a live case with three cloned VMs. The full command sequence is in the article.

item.title: Atomic MacOS (AMOS) stealer infection, (Sun, Aug 2nd)
item.description:
AMOS stealer is spreading via fake "macOS toolkit" paste-in-Terminal lures, dropping persistent Mach-O binaries disguised as Apple system processes with C2 over plain HTTP to 188.166.78[.]138.
- The infection chain starts at getmacouscloud[.]com, which serves base64-encoded text users are told to paste into Terminal. That text fetches a zsh script (SHA256: b9ec3261...) from render65[.]com, which unpacks a second zsh stage that drops and executes the AMOS Mach-O binary from /tmp/helper. Classic ClickFix/paste-lure technique, no exploit required, just social engineering.
- AMOS persists by copying itself into hidden Apple-lookalike paths: /Users/[username]/Library/Application Support/.com.apple.accountsd/AccountsHelper and .com.apple.metadata.mds/mdworker_shared. Both are universal Mach-O binaries supporting x86_64 and arm64, meaning M-series and Intel Macs are both targeted.
- C2 runs over plain HTTP port 80 to 188.166.78[.]138, cycling through staged beacon endpoints: boot, init_session, credentials, browsers, wallets, local_data. That enumeration order tells the story: credentials and crypto wallets are the primary targets.
Hunt for unsigned Mach-O binaries in Library/Application Support paths beginning with a dot, and flag outbound plain HTTP from user-space processes. Full IOC list including five SHA256 hashes and all defanged URLs is in the SANS ISC report.

item.title: Analyzing Nova Ransomware: A Rust-Based Encryptor with Multi-Layered Microsoft Defender Evasion Techniques
item.description:
Nova ransomware is a Rust-based RaaS encryptor combining multi-layered Microsoft Defender tampering, shadow copy deletion, and hybrid XChaCha20-Poly1305/RSA-2048 encryption to maximize damage before detection fires.
Key findings:
- Nova disables Microsoft Defender through direct tampering before encryption begins, then terminates security-related processes to clear the path. The Rust implementation complicates static analysis and signature matching compared to more common C/C++ ransomware.
- Encryption uses a hybrid scheme: XChaCha20-Poly1305 for file contents and RSA-2048 for key protection. This combination is cryptographically sound and makes recovery without the private key mathematically infeasible.
- Volume Shadow Copies are deleted as part of the execution chain (T1490), eliminating the most common on-host recovery path. Recovery inhibition is baked into the attack flow, not an afterthought.
- Anti-analysis techniques are present throughout, slowing dynamic sandbox detonation and manual reverse engineering.
Defenders should prioritize detections on VSS deletion via vssadmin or WMI, Defender tamper protection bypasses, and security process termination events. AttackIQ has published an adversary emulation covering Nova's TTPs so teams can validate whether those controls actually fire before a real intrusion does.
